title: Relatedness Lives in the Common Ancestor

scenes.tts: A trout is more closely related to you than to a shark. That sounds wrong, because trout and shark both look like fish. So how can a tree show it? A phylogenetic tree is a branching diagram of hypothesized ancestry. The living species sit at its tips.
scenes.visual: Trout, shark and human dots; a look-alike bracket joins trout and shark; a question mark sits over the trout-human link; the words phylogenetic tree appear.
scenes.narration: A trout is more closely related to you than to a shark. That sounds wrong, because trout and shark both look like fish. So how can a tree show it? A phylogenetic tree is a branching diagram of hypothesized ancestry. The living species sit at its tips.

scenes.tts: Here is a rooted tree of five animals. The lamprey is the outgroup, a taxon assumed to lie outside the group being studied. Each place where a branch splits is a node. A node stands for an inferred common ancestor of every lineage above it. The root is the ancestor of everything on the tree.
scenes.visual: The five-tip tree draws itself with level tips; lamprey is tagged outgroup; nodes R, J, B, T light up in turn; the root is marked.
scenes.narration: Here is a rooted tree of five animals. The lamprey is the outgroup, a taxon assumed to lie outside the group being studied. Each place where a branch splits is a node. A node stands for an inferred common ancestor of every lineage above it. The root is the ancestor of everything on the tree.

scenes.tts: To compare two tips, trace each one back until their lines meet. Trout and human meet at node B. Trout and shark meet at node J. Node J is older, because J is ancestral to B. The most recent common ancestor is the latest node from which both descend. So trout is more closely related to human, and equally to frog.
scenes.visual: A yellow path traces trout and human back to B, then trout and shark back to J; B is ringed as the more recent meeting point; frog joins human.
scenes.narration: To compare two tips, trace each one back until their lines meet. Trout and human meet at node B. Trout and shark meet at node J. Node J is older, because J is ancestral to B. The most recent common ancestor is the latest node from which both descend. So trout is more closely related to human, and equally to frog.

scenes.tts: Now spin node T, so that human is drawn above frog. The node still has the same two descendants. A clade is an ancestor and all of its descendants, and every clade has the same members. So the relationships have not changed. Spin node B as well, and shark no longer sits beside trout. Tips that sit side by side on the page are not, for that reason, closest relatives. The sister group of trout is the frog and human clade.
scenes.visual: Node T rotates (frog and human swap rows), then node B rotates (shark no longer beside trout); a green no-change tag stays; the frog-human clade is boxed as trout's sister group.
scenes.narration: Now spin node T, so that human is drawn above frog. The node still has the same two descendants. A clade is an ancestor and all of its descendants, and every clade has the same members. So the relationships have not changed. Spin node B as well, and shark no longer sits beside trout. Tips that sit side by side on the page are not, for that reason, closest relatives. The sister group of trout is the frog and human clade.

scenes.tts: Do not count nodes either. The number of nodes between two tips depends on which other species were sampled. Add five more fish, and the count between trout and human rises. Their most recent common ancestor has not moved. Nor is any living tip more evolved than another. The human and trout lineages have each been evolving since node B. Lampreys are not primitive animals.
scenes.visual: Five fish tips are added on the trout side, extra nodes light up between trout and B while B stays ringed; then the original tree returns with two equal arrows from B to trout and human, and struck-out tags more evolved and primitive.
scenes.narration: Do not count nodes either. The number of nodes between two tips depends on which other species were sampled. Add five more fish, and the count between trout and human rises. Their most recent common ancestor has not moved. Nor is any living tip more evolved than another. The human and trout lineages have each been evolving since node B. Lampreys are not primitive animals.

scenes.tts: A tree is a hypothesis about ancestry. Nobody watched these lineages split. The tree is estimated from characters, usually DNA or protein sequences, and it can be tested and overturned. So keep one rule. Find the most recent common ancestor. Do not judge relatedness by how the tips sit on the page.
scenes.visual: The tree is spun at several nodes while a yellow ring stays on node B; the rule appears beneath it.
